title: The covariance matrix
summary: C = XᵀX/(n − 1): every variance from one symmetric 2×2 matrix.

blocks.title: XᵀX

define.meaning: For the $5 \times 2$ matrix $X$, a $2 \times 2$ matrix: row $i$, column $j$ is (column $i$ of $X$) · (column $j$ of $X$). The same bookkeeping as $A^\mathsf{T}A$ in least squares.

blocks.why: Scoring each direction point by point is slow. $X^\mathsf{T}X$ does all the adding once, for every direction at the same time.

slips.say: That is $P^\mathsf{T}P$ from the raw points. Use the centred ones, the rows of $X$.

hints: Row 1, column 1 is column 1 · column 1: the sum of squares of the centred $x$'s, which you have already found.
That dot product is $0 + 2 - 2 + 2 + 6$. Row 2, column 2 is $0 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4$.

check.say: $X^\mathsf{T}X$ equals its own transpose, so the two off-diagonal entries must match. Add the products one at a time in the calculator.

blocks.solution: Symmetric, as it must be. The diagonal holds the sums of squares you found point by point.

blocks.title: The covariance matrix C

define.meaning: $C = \frac{1}{n-1}X^\mathsf{T}X$, for centred $X$. Its diagonal entries are the variances along the axes; the off-diagonal entry is the covariance of $x$ and $y$.

blocks.why: Dividing by $n - 1$ turns sums of squares into variances, the same convention as the last lesson.

slips.say: That comes from the raw points. Centre first: $C$ is built from $X$.

hints: Divide every entry of $X^\mathsf{T}X$ by the same number.

check.say: The diagonal should be your two variances from the last lesson, along $(1, 0)$ and $(0, 1)$.

blocks.solution: The covariance 2 is positive: when a point is right of the mean it tends to be above it too. That is the lean you saw.

blocks.title: Variance along u from C

define.meaning: For a unit $u$: $u^\mathsf{T}Cu = \frac{1}{n-1}\,u^\mathsf{T}X^\mathsf{T}Xu = \frac{1}{n-1}\|Xu\|^2$, and $Xu$ lists the five $x_i \cdot u$. So it is the variance along $u$.

blocks.why: This is the payoff: one small matrix gives the variance along any direction, without going back to the points.

slips.say: That is $w^\mathsf{T}Cw$ for $w = (1, 1)$. Use the unit vector: its two factors $1/\sqrt2$ halve it.

hints: Work with $w = (1, 1)$ first: compute $Cw$, then $w \cdot Cw$.

check.say: It should be the variance along the diagonal you found in the last lesson from the five points.

blocks.solution: The same 7.5, from a $2 \times 2$ matrix instead of five dot products.

blocks.title: The total variance

define.meaning: $\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_i \|x_i\|^2$: how spread out the points are in all directions together.

blocks.why: Each point's $\|x_i\|^2$ splits into a part along a line and a part across it (Pythagoras). So any direction and its perpendicular share the same total.
blocks.prompt: What is the total variance of the five centred points?

widget.name: pca-scatter
widget.caption: The dashed line is perpendicular to the solid one. Turn them: the two variances change, their sum does not.

slips.say: That is the sum of squares. Now divide by $n - 1$.
That adds all four entries of $C$. The total is the diagonal only: $C_{11} + C_{22}$.

hints: $\|x_i\|^2 = x^2 + y^2$ for each centred point. Add all five, then divide by $n - 1$.
Or add the variance along $(1, 0)$ and along $(0, 1)$: the diagonal of $C$.

check.say: The picture's last line adds the two variances; it should show your total at every angle.

blocks.solution: 11, whatever pair of perpendicular directions you use. The best direction takes as much of 11 as it can, and leaves the rest to its perpendicular.

sideQuest.title: Check it in numpy
sideQuest.body:
Only if you want to.

```
import numpy as np
P = np.array([[0, 2], [3, 0], [5, 0], [5, 4], [7, 4]])
print(np.cov(P, rowvar=False))  # [[7, 2], [2, 4]]; np.cov divides by n - 1
```
